name: Phubbing
summary: The act of snubbing someone in a social setting by focusing on one's phone instead of the person.
explanation:
Phubbing is a blend of the words "phone" and "snubbing." It describes the increasingly common behavior of ignoring the people physically present with you in favor of your smartphone, whether to check notifications, scroll social media, or reply to messages. The term was popularized around 2012 as part of a campaign to name a behavior that many people recognized but had no vocabulary for, and it has since become a widely studied phenomenon in social psychology.

The behavior is corrosive precisely because it is so casual and habitual. A quick glance at a screen mid-conversation signals, often unintentionally, that whatever is happening on the phone matters more than the person in front of you. Because phones are designed to capture attention through variable rewards and constant alerts, the pull toward them is strong even when we consciously value the face-to-face interaction more. The result is that presence becomes fragmented and shallow, and the people around us feel the difference even when we do not notice we are doing it.

Research links phubbing to lower relationship satisfaction, reduced feelings of connection, and diminished conversation quality. When one partner regularly phubs the other, it can erode trust and intimacy over time, a pattern researchers sometimes call "partner phubbing." Even the mere presence of a phone on the table, without it being used, has been shown to reduce how meaningful and empathetic a conversation feels. The behavior also tends to be reciprocal and normalizing: seeing others phub makes us more likely to do it ourselves, gradually lowering the shared standard for attentiveness.

Addressing phubbing is less about willpower in the moment and more about designing situations where the temptation is removed. Practical countermeasures include keeping phones out of sight during meals and conversations, silencing notifications, and establishing explicit norms with friends, family, or colleagues about device-free time. On a deeper level, resisting phubbing is an exercise in valuing sustained, undistracted attention as a form of respect and care, treating the people we are with as more deserving of our focus than the endless stream of digital input competing for it.
